caption: A, Magnetic resonance image of the breasts shows an enhancing 5.2-cm left axillary mass (arrowhead) but no breast lesions. B, Immunohistochemical staining revealed tumor cells positive for PAX8 (original magnification ×100).
scenario: A 76-year-old woman presented with a palpable left axillary mass. When she was 36 years old, she underwent a hysterectomy due to abnormal uterine bleeding and was taking estradiol to control postmenopausal vasomotor symptoms for the past 20 years. Bilateral diagnostic mammography revealed a high-density irregular mass in the left axilla with no nodules, architectural distortions, or microcalcifications in the breasts. Ultrasonography of the left breast showed a 4.6-cm lobulated mixed cystic and solid left axillary mass. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging showed an enhancing 5.2-cm left axillary mass with no breast lesions (Figure 1A). The biopsy examination indicated high-grade adenocarcinoma with papillary features (estrogen receptor– and progesterone receptor–positive, ERBB2 [formerly HER2]–negative, and a high Ki67 index). Positron emission tomography/computed tomography revealed only high uptake in the left axilla region. The patient was treated at an outside hospital with neoadjuvant dose-dense doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide, followed by weekly paclitaxel for 10 weeks. She then transferred her care to our center for surgical management. We requested the pathology slides for review at our laboratory and additional immunostaining was performed, which revealed high-grade adenocarcinoma with tumor cells positive for PAX8 (Figure 1B), p53, and WT1 and negative for GATA3.

options.B: High-grade serous carcinoma of gynecological origin
options.C: High-grade carcinoma of the breast with occult primary
options.D: High-grade papillary carcinoma of unknown primary

answer: High-grade serous carcinoma of gynecological origin
distractors: High-grade carcinoma of the breast with occult primary
High-grade papillary carcinoma of unknown primary
explanation: B. High-grade serous carcinoma of gynecological origin This patient underwent left axillary excisional lymph node biopsy, peritoneal washings, laparoscopic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omental biopsy, and bilateral ureterolysis. Laparoscopy revealed that both ovaries were affixed to the pelvic peritoneum with adhesions, requiring bilateral ureterolysis. The uterus, cervix, and proximal fallopian tubes were surgically absent. On gross examination the distal fallopian tubes appeared unremarkable, and the left ovary appeared nodular. Given the clinical scenario, the fimbrial ends of the fallopian tubes were entirely excised and submitted for microscopic examination along with both ovaries. Microscopic examination revealed a residual 2.1-mm focus of high-grade serous carcinoma (Figure 2) involving the fimbrial end of the left fallopian tube. No omental involvement was seen. The immunostaining pattern was similar to that seen in the axillary metastasis prior to therapy. No residual carcinoma was identified in the left axillary lymph node. The patient’s cancer antigen 125 level was 13 U/mL before the surgery. Disease was staged as FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) stage IVB, and the patient received additional platinum-based adjuvant chemotherapy. Test results were negative for germline pathogenic sequence variants, includingBRCA1andBRCA2. Although metastatic ovarian or tubal serous carcinoma typically first spreads locally within the abdomen or peritoneum, distal extra-abdominal involvement is well established.1An isolated axillary mass rarely presents as the initial sign of ovarian or tubal serous carcinoma, and there are few cases reported.2-4Unlike other patients, this patient was initially treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy with a presumptive diagnosis of an occult breast cancer with axillary metastasis. After histopathologic reassessment and additional immunostaining at our institution, the treatment plan was adjusted accordingly. Her initial diagnostic evaluation included clinical history, radiography, and pathologic examination. Given the pathologic findings, location of the malignant neoplasm, and positive hormone receptor expression, this case was misdiagnosed as breast cancer at the outside institution. Immunohistochemical staining was key to reaching the correct diagnosis. Clinical management of axillary nodal metastases of carcinoma of unknown primary (CUPAx) is challenging. A systematic review reported that 72% of the patients with CUPAx treated with prophylactic mastectomy had an occult primary cancer of the breast,5which implied that a thorough investigation of breast origin might be appropriate and could avoid unnecessary surgeries. In these situations, immunostaining can offer more insight but only to a limited extent. Greco et al6evaluated diagnoses based on molecular profile, immunostaining (median of 6 stains), and clinical findings, and reported that diagnoses among all 3 modalities were consistent for only 34% of the patients. Some markers may provide evidence implying the primary site; for example, TTF-1 and thyroglobulin are relatively specific for thyroid cancer, CK7 and GATA3 are highly suggestive of breast cancer, and CK7, WT1, and PAX8 are indicative of gynecological adenocarcinoma.7,8While estrogen and progesterone receptors are frequently evaluated in breast cancers, they can also be expressed in ovarian cancer, and some evidence supports their prognostic value.9,10Thus, infradiaphragmatic primary malignant neoplasm should not be completely excluded when positive hormone profiles are present. Ovarian serous papillary adenocarcinoma initially presenting as axillary lymph node metastasis is rare. When managing CUPAx, primary sites other than the breast should be explored. Thorough clinical history, physical examination, and histopathologic evaluation of the biopsy specimen in conjunction with immunostaining is invaluable in establishing a diagnosis.

scenario: A man in his early 70s with a history of permanent atrial fibrillation treated with atrioventricular junction ablation and biventricular pacemaker implantation was hospitalized with decompensated heart failure and acute kidney injury. His history was notable for nonischemic cardiomyopathy with ejection fraction of 40% and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, for which he underwent single-lung transplant 9 years prior. Following diuresis and medical optimization, repeated echocardiogram showed a newly depressed ejection fraction (30%). His electrocardiogram (ECG) was notable for alternating QRS morphologies (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) pacing vector was programmed from LV tip to right ventricular (RV) lead ring. During pacemaker threshold testing, a change in QRS morphology was observed as the output was reduced (Figure 1B). Chest radiography revealed severe right pulmonary fibrosis leading to ipsilateral mediastinal shift and pacemaker lead position unchanged from implantation.
explanation: C. Change the LV pacing configuration The diagnosis of anodal capture is strongly suggested by the sudden change in QRS configuration during the LV threshold test (Figure 1B). Further, LV pacing should produce a right bundle branch block morphology (predominantly positive QRS in V1), which is not observed and raises the possibility of anodal capture. In the above LV threshold test, the paced vector (from LV lead to RV lead) resulted in concurrent capture of both the LV and RV tissue at high output. At diminishing output, left ventricular capture was lost while RV capture (anodal capture) persisted. This RV capture QRS morphology was identical to the QRS morphology when pacing from the RV lead. This is consistent with anodal stimulation, defined as pure or predominant RV capture when LV pacing. Cardiac electrical dyssynchrony is a cause of mechanical inefficiency and worsening heart failure. Placement of RV and LV leads allows for electrical resynchronization with a biventricular pacemaker. LV leads can pace in multiple configurations to avoid phrenic nerve capture or areas of scar. One common pacing configuration is to drive electrical current from the LV lead (cathode) to the RV lead (anode). When the LV tissue is diseased and difficult to excite electrically, this pacing configuration is susceptible to RV myocardial capture without LV myocardial excitation,1,2a phenomenon originally termedanodal capture.3 Identification of anodal capture requires close examination of the surface ECG by the treating physician. A biventricular pacemaker is unable to detect this phenomenon and will give a false sense of reassurance that resynchronization is occurring. In this patient’s case, device interrogation suggested that effective biventricular pacing was occurring 98% of the time while the surface ECG demonstrated that this number was closer to 66%. Previous studies have demonstrated that unrecognized anodal capture can account for failure to respond to resynchronization therapy.4,5The preferred treatment for this problem is to adjust the pacing configuration to exclude the RV lead. Of note, while this patient had a bipolar LV lead, more modern quadripolar LV leads allow multiple LV-only pacing configurations that prevent anodal capture by obviating LV to RV pacing. Finally, anodal capture is seen almost exclusively in pacemakers as the large defibrillation coil in implantable cardioverter-defibrillator leads requires much higher current to excite the RV myocardium.6 For this patient, the LV pacing configuration was changed to a true bipolar LV configuration (LV distal to proximal electrode) and a pure LV capture morphology was observed (Figure 2). Unfortunately, the patient died of complications from recurrent diverticulitis with perforation, precluding repeated echocardiographic assessment of his cardiomyopathy following adjustment of his pacing configuration.

Right, Maxillary sinus biopsy sample revealing numerous broad, nonseptate right-angled hyphae and fruiting bodies (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400).
scenario: A 41-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and a hemoglobin A1clevel of 16.8% (reference, 4.0%-5.6%) 1 month prior to admission presented to the emergency department with 1 week of generalized weakness. His temperature was 38.5 °C (101.3 °F); blood pressure, 125/75 mm Hg; heart rate, 95/min; respiratory rate, 24/min; and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. His voice was muffled and his speech was dysarthric. He appeared lethargic but had no focal neurologic deficits. Physical examination findings were normal except for tonsillar edema. White blood cell count was 13.4 ×103/μL (reference, 4-11 ×103/μL); blood glucose level, 274 mg/dL (15.21 mmol/L) (reference, 70-100 mg/dL [3.89-5.55 mmol/L]); serum creatinine level, 0.9 mg/dL (79.56 μmol/L) (reference, 0.4-1.3 mg/dL [35.36-114.92 μmol/L]); bicarbonate level, 9 mmol/L (reference, 20-30 mmol/L); arterial pH, 7.21 (reference, 7.35-7.45); β-hydroxybutyric acid level, 58.2 mg/dL (5590 μmol/L) (reference, <2.81 mg/dL [269.9 μmol/L]); and serum anion gap, 21 (reference, 7-17). Findings on a chest radiograph were normal. A computed tomography scan of the head and neck with intravenous contrast showed mucosal thickening of the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, and prominence of the adenoids and palatine tonsils. Flexible laryngoscopy showed patent nasal sinuses and mucosal edema without abscess or necrosis. He was treated with intravenous fluids and with insulin, vancomycin (1 g intravenously every 12 hours), and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g intravenously every 6 hours). On hospital day 2, his temperature was 38.9 °C (102 °F). A repeat computed tomography scan of the neck demonstrated soft-tissue gas in the nasopharynx and prevertebral fascia (Figure, left panel). Flexible laryngoscopy revealed necrotic tissue throughout the nasopharynx. Emergent transnasal endoscopic debridement of the maxillary, sphenoid, and ethmoid sinuses was performed. Sinus mucosal samples grewCandida albicansin fungal cultures, and histopathology identified numerous broad, nonseptate right-angled hyphae and fruiting bodies (Figure, right panel).

options.A: Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily)
options.C: Order fluconazole (200 mg orally daily for 14 days)
options.D: Prescribe prednisone (40 mg orally daily for 5 days)

answer: Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily)
distractors: Order fluconazole (200 mg orally daily for 14 days)
Prescribe prednisone (40 mg orally daily for 5 days)
explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

scenario: A man in his 40s was seen in clinic for a long history of palpitations. He had a history of cardiac arrest after receiving adenosine for sustained supraventricular tachycardia and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. The patient was also noted to have episodes of atrial flutter. Transthoracic echocardiogram displayed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 63% and mild aortic and mitral regurgitation. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging in sinus rhythm showed mild left ventricle thickening (up to 14 mm) and was otherwise normal. The patient was hospitalized for initiation of sotalol, given that he experienced frequent episodes of atrial arrhythmia.Figure 1A shows sinus rhythm prior to sotalol initiation.Figure 1B shows telemetry during administration of sotalol.
explanation: Latent accessory pathway (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) B. Electrophysiology study and catheter ablation Prior to sotalol loading, the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) (Figure1A) showed sinus rhythm at 57 beats per minute with a normal axis and QT interval. There were no Q waves in the lateral leads. There were inferolateral precordial T-wave abnormalities. With sotalol loading, the telemetry strip (Figure1B) revealed widening of the QRS complex. The differential diagnosis included (1) rate-related aberrancy, (2) idioventricular rhythm, (3) phase 4 aberrancy, and (4) preexcitation from an atrioventricular pathway. Phase 3 or 4 aberrancy was unlikely because the sinus rate had not changed significantly. An idioventricular rhythm resulting in this finding would have to be perfectly isorhythmic to maintain constant PR intervals. The short, fixed PR interval with wide QRS complex makes ventricular preexcitation from an atrioventricular pathway (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) the most likely diagnosis.1Electrophysiology study and catheter ablation provide high likelihood of cure. Amiodarone is not indicated in a young patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome; ST segment changes are due to altered ventricular repolarization owing to preexcitation rather than ischemia. Exercise treadmill testing is not useful with lack of ischemia or exposure to medications with use dependence (class I). The ECG initially did not show clear ventricular preexcitation. An accessory pathway that is not capable of antegrade conduction will not be apparent on an ECG in sinus rhythm; this is termedconcealed preexcitation.2However, with sotalol loading, anterograde conduction with delta waves develops in this patient without a change in heart rate. Absent delta waves in the presence of an accessory pathway capable of anterograde conduction has been termedlatent preexcitation.3The proposed mechanism for this phenomenon is due to relative conduction times from the sinus node through the atrioventricular node vs across the atrium and the accessory pathway. Conditions that may cause latent preexcitation include left-lateral pathways, delay in intra-atrial conduction time, or increased left-atrial size. Some evidence exists that this phenomenon may occur when autonomic influences on the pathway and on atrioventricular nodal conduction are opposite.4Additionally, concealed retrograde conduction into the accessory pathway during sinus rhythm could prevent preexcitation and eliminate delta waves. Sotalol has been studied for treatment of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia  in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome but has not been reported to reveal a latent accessory pathway. Sotalol causes an increase in the retrograde effective refractory period of accessory pathways, whereas changes in the anterograde refractory periods were more variable.5,6It is unlikely that sotalol improved conduction in the accessory pathway. Instead, sotalol slows atrioventricular nodal conduction and may prevent concealed retrograde conduction into the pathway in a manner analogous to transseptal concealed conduction for perpetuation of bundle-branch block. Repeated 12-lead ECG confirmed manifest preexcitation (short PR intervals and delta waves,Figure 2). Negative delta waves in leads II, III, and aVF and QRS transition between V1and V2argues for a posteroseptal pathway.7The patient then developed a narrow-complex short RP tachycardia showing negative P waves in the inferior leads consistent with a posterior accessory pathway-mediated orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia. The tachycardia was terminated with the Valsalva maneuver. After providing consent, the patient underwent successful catheter ablation of the posteroseptal pathway and cavotricuspid isthmus (for typical right-atrial flutter). The successful ablation site was the anterior floor of the coronary sinus body, about 1 to 2 cm from the coronary sinus ostium. Sotalol treatment was discontinued, and the patient was discharged with metoprolol and lisinopril therapy.

scenario: A patient in their 20s presented to the emergency department with presyncope, hives, and nausea after walking outside in the cold. On arrival, their pulse was 120 beats per minute; blood pressure, 85/52 mm Hg; respiratory rate, 20 breaths per minute; oxygen saturation, 100% with a nonrebreather mask; and temperature, 36.8° C. The patient was in moderate respiratory distress, and chest auscultation revealed bilateral wheezing. They were treated for presumed anaphylaxis with 0.5 mg of epinephrine intramuscularly. Immediately after the administration of epinephrine, they developed a headache, nausea, and chest pain. A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) was obtained 5 minutes later (Figure 1). The patient had persistent hypotension.

options.C: Give a second dose of 0.5 mg of intramuscular epinephrine
options.D: Administer 100 to 200 µg of intravenous phenylephrine

answer: Give a second dose of 0.5 mg of intramuscular epinephrine
distractors: Administer 100 to 200 µg of intravenous phenylephrine
explanation: Kounis syndrome (acute coronary vasospasm associated with anaphylactoid response) C. Give a second dose of 0.5 mg of intramuscular epinephrine Kounis syndrome is a pathological state of acute coronary vasospasm with mast cell degranulation and interaction with other inflammatory cells secondary to allergic or hypersensitivity and anaphylactic or anaphylactoid insults.1,2The inflammatory mediators involved include histamine, arachidonic acid, neutral protease, and platelet-activating factors.1,3Coronary arteries can be the primary site during anaphylaxis and result in Kounis syndrome manifestations.1,3Kounis syndrome can be precipitated by many factors, including angioedema, urticaria, hay fever, food allergy,Hymenopterastings, latex, and drugs.1,2 Three variants of Kounis syndrome have been described. Type 1 includes patients with normal or near-normal coronary arteries without predisposing factors for coronary artery disease, in whom the acute release of inflammatory mediators induce coronary artery spasm attributable to endothelial dysfunction with or without an increase of cardiac enzymes and troponins.1Type 2 includes quiescent preexisting atheromatous disease, in whom acute release of inflammatory mediators induce coronary artery spasm with plaque erosion or rupture, manifesting as acute myocardial infarction.1,4Type 3 includes patients with coronary artery stent thrombosis.4 A high index of suspicion is of paramount importance, since the diagnosis might be easily overlooked.5In the settings of allergic reactions, the presence of a cardiac symptom profile, such as acute chest pain, chest discomfort, dyspnea, palpitations, tachycardia or bradycardia, hypotension, cold extremities, diaphoresis, or cardiac arrest, must raise the suspicion for Kounis syndrome.1 The ECG may show a variety of abnormalities, including ST-segment depression or elevation, atrial fibrillation, sinus bradycardia or tachycardia, T-wave flattening or inversion, atrioventricular block, bigeminal rhythm, ventricular ectopic beats, and ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation.1Serum levels of tryptase are elevated during an episode.3However, cardiac injury biomarkers, such as cardiac enzymes and troponins, may or may not be elevated.3 The management of Kounis syndrome includes treatment of both anaphylactic shock (initially with intramuscular epinephrine) and acute coronary syndrome.4Type 1 is managed with intravenous corticosteroids, H1 and H2 antihistamines, and analgesia. Type 2 is managed as per the acute coronary event protocol, along with corticosteroids and antihistamines. Type 3 requires urgent harvest of the intrastent thrombus along with corticosteroids and antihistamines. The use of additional drugs must be done cautiously, because nitroglycerine causes hypotension, β-blockers can cause coronary artery spasm, and morphine might result in mast cell degranulation.5After the resolution of the acute event, a full cardiology workup, including 12-lead ECG, echocardiogram, and evaluation for modifiable cardiac risk factors, must be performed, along with follow-up with an allergy or immunology specialist.3 The patient’s presentation was consistent with anaphylaxis and possibly cold-induced urticaria. In the emergency department, they were treated with intramuscular epinephrine, methylprednisolone, ondansetron, diphenhydramine, and famotidine, with improvement. After the resolution of symptoms, a repeated ECG showed resolution of a multilead ST-segment depression (Figure 2). The patient had normal biochemistry test results, except for an elevated high-sensitivity troponin I level of 486.0 ng/L (normal range, ≤26 ng/L; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1.0), which normalized within 16 hours during admission. The presentation was consistent with Kounis syndrome or anaphylactic coronary artery vasospasm, given the presence of anaphylaxis and ECG changes. They had an uncomplicated short admission to the internal medicine service. After consultation with the cardiology service, it was decided not to pursue coronary angiography, since symptoms had resolved and ECG and troponin results had normalized. On discharge, they were referred to an allergist and a medical genetics consultant, with instructions to carry an EpiPen always.

scenario: A 56-year-old woman presented at the clinic for follow-up of metastatic hormone receptor–positive,ERBB2-negative breast cancer. She had locally advanced disease that was invading the skin overlying her right breast and metastatic disease to the thoracic and lumbar spine, liver, and mediastinal, axillary, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Her disease had progressed after receiving first-line therapy with palbociclib and anastrozole. Subsequent treatments with fulvestrant and paclitaxel were also followed by progressive disease. She received treatment with capecitabine; after 6 weeks of treatment, she developed some redness on her hands and feet that resolved on its own. She then presented to the clinic with pruritic, erythematous, scaly macules and papules on her forearms, faces, chest, and upper back (Figure). The rash had been present for 3 weeks and had recently worsened. Her palms and soles were spared. The rash did not respond to treatment with topical clindamycin, oral solumedrol, or doxycycline. She had a history of substantial sun exposure but no history of skin cancer.

options.A: Cutaneous deposits of metastatic breast cancer

distractors: Cutaneous deposits of metastatic breast cancer
explanation: B. Inflammation of actinic keratoses Capecitabine is an orally bioavailable prodrug of fluorouracil that was initially approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for treating breast and colorectal cancer and has since gained additional indications for various solid tumor cancers. After metabolism to active fluorouracil in the target tissue, the drug exhibits a cytotoxic effect through incorporation within the DNA, which is followed by strand breaks, inhibition of RNA synthesis, and inhibition of thymidylate synthase.1,2There are several cutaneous adverse effects associated with capecitabine, such as palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, vitiligo, pruritus, dermatitis, alopecia, onycholysis, and the inflammation of preexisting actinic keratoses (AKs). Actinic keratoses result from atypical proliferation of keratinocytes, with the potential for malignant transformation. They occur predominantly on chronic sun-exposed skin areas, such as the balding scalp, face, and dorsal forearms and hands, and are the most common premalignant skin condition in elderly individuals.2Many treatments exist for AKs, of which one of the most used and successful is topical fluorouracil.3 Shortly after US Food and Drug Administration approval, cases describing inflammation of AKs in patients undergoing treatment with capecitabine were published.2-6In 2020, a systemic review described the available evidence for the use of capecitabine for preventing and treating AKs, as well as its use for chemoprevention of cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas in solid organ transplant recipients.7The review comprised 8 case reports of AK inflammation, with the onset of dermatologic changes ranging from 4 days to 6 weeks after receiving treatment with capecitabine. After initial inflammation of the AK lesions, the typical course includes gradual healing and disappearance during the coming days to weeks. In described cases, some patients were prescribed topical corticosteroids for symptomatic relief, but its use was not universal. Antoniolli and colleagues8published a similar literature review and described a tendency for older studies to have included discontinuation of the drug, with a trend toward a treat through approach more recently. In all cases that reported outcomes, there was a partial or complete resolution of the inflammation of the AKs. Thus, this effect should potentially be considered therapeutic, and treatment with capecitabine should not necessarily be discontinued. The underlying mechanism for the inflammation of AKs with capecitabine is similar to the direct cytotoxic effect seen in any cancer treated with fluorouracil. The interference of DNA and RNA synthesis via inhibition of thymidylate synthase that causes double-stranded DNA breaks is key to its cytotoxic mechanism of action.1,9When administered systemically, capecitabine exhibits preferential accumulation in areas of active cell proliferation.8This is associated with amplified responses in the skin and the resultant inflammation of AKs, while sparing normal skin. A pathologically distinct yet phenotypically similar phenomenon has been described in radiation recall dermatitis. It is defined as the recalling of an effect that is similar to an acute radiation reaction in an area of previous irradiation.10Capecitabine has been a medication recently implicated in this phenomenon.10The underlying pathophysiology is poorly understood, but it is theorized that upregulation of thymidine phosphorylase plays a role in the neoangiogenesis and preferential accumulation of capecitabine in previously irradiated tissue. The current patient was prescribed triamcinolone, 0.1%, cream for symptomatic relief. She did not experience further episodes of inflammation with subsequent treatment cycles of capecitabine, and the skin lesions eventually resolved.

caption: Computed tomography (CT) images of 2 brothers with bilateral lesions in the olfactory clefts. A, Cone-beam CT in the 69-year-old brother demonstrated significant widening of the olfactory clefts and right-sided bony thinning. B, Reformatted conventional CT scan in the 76-year-old brother showed similar findings.
scenario: Two brothers, aged 69 and 76 years, were independently referred to our center in the same week for evaluation of a right olfactory cleft tumor that had been progressively developing over several years. The brothers had not been in contact with each other for many years. Neither had a history of chronic rhinosinusitis. The 69-year-old patient had a medical history of benign prostatic hypertrophy and prior septoplasty. The 76-year-old brother had no relevant medical or surgical history. Both brothers reported an ipsilateral nasal obstruction, with no other significant symptoms. Clinical examination on both patients revealed a lesion originating from the right olfactory cleft. Imaging studies were performed to further characterize the findings. A computed tomography scan demonstrated bilateral masses causing widening of the olfactory clefts, with the right-sided lesion being larger than the left and causing nasal bone thinning in both patients (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a smooth, larger, right-sided lesion in the olfactory clefts with heterogeneous T2 signal and heterogenous contrast enhancement, along with a smaller lesion on the left side.
explanation: After initial evaluation and imaging, both patients underwent surgical resection of the tumor in the right olfactory cleft to improve their nasal breathing and for pathological examination. A biopsy of the lesion located in the left olfactory cleft for both patients was also performed. Pathological examination revealed a similar finding in both brothers: a polypoid formation with dystrophic respiratory glands, sometimes with intestinal metaplasia and sometimes with ciliated lining, anarchically distributed within the chorion, without adenomatous or atypical character. This histopathological presentation strongly supports the diagnosis of respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), despite the absence of genetic analysis.1,2 Olfactory cleft hamartomas are benign tumors that may be isolated or associated with chronic rhinosinusitis. They typically appear as a smooth polypoid mass in the anterior part of the nasal cavity. These lesions predominantly affect men, with a male to female ratio of 7:2.2The olfactory cleft is the most common site for hamartoma, followed by the posterior region of the septum. Both nasal cavities are involved in most cases (53%).3On imaging, hamartomas are usually seen as exophytic polypoid homogeneous lesions with smooth expansion of the olfactory cleft without bony erosion and exhibiting a characteristic crescentic half-moon appearance on the sagittal views when the lesion is situated along the olfactory cleft.4 The 5th World Health Organization Classification identifies 3 types of hamartomas: REAH, seromucinous hamartoma, and nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma (CMH). Pathological examination and molecular analysis are essential for differentiation, as REAH and seromucinous hamartoma cannot be distinguished based on imaging alone. CMHs are usually found in infants and contain mixed mesenchymal elements, including cartilage. CMH can be associated with aDICER1(tumor-suppressor gene) variant.4,5 There is currently no cause identified for isolated REAH, but research is limited. Some evidence suggests that hamartomas may arise secondary to inflammatory processes, such as chronic rhinosinusitis.3A congenital cause is also suspected, but no genetic basis has been identified yet. It is quite rare to see similar isolated REAH in 2 brothers without any associated inflammatory conditions. This clinical case raises the possibility of an unknown underlying genetic mechanism. Treatment is symptom dependent. Surgical removal is often performed in cases of nasal obstruction or to restore olfactory function, with a high success rate and a low risk of recurrence.1,3While surgery is not always necessary, a biopsy is recommended when imaging findings are inconclusive to rule out other potential diagnoses. Differentials diagnosis include Schneiderian papilloma, sinonasal adenocarcinoma, or olfactory neuroblastoma. Imaging often helps to differentiate REAH from other diagnoses. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, nasal polyps typically originate from the ethmoid sinuses, whereas the imaging here clearly shows a lesion widening the olfactory cleft (Figure 2). Schneiderian papillomas are rarely bilateral and typically exhibit a more irregular or lobulated appearance on T2-weighted imaging, often accompanied by bone remodeling at the attachment point or bone erosion—features that are absent in this case. Malignant tumors, such as ethmoid sinus adenocarcinoma, typically demonstrate aggressive characteristics, including bone destruction, heterogeneous enhancement, and invasion of adjacent structures, none of which were observed here. Finally, encephaloceles are characterized by herniation of intracranial contents into the nasal cavity and are commonly associated with skull base defects, which are not identified in these images.

scenario: A woman in her 60s was diagnosed with high-grade leiomyosarcoma of the uterus in 2017 for which she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. In 2020, she relapsed in the liver and spine. In November 2020, she underwent posterior lateral stabilization of C7-T4 for a T2 vertebral body metastasis causing cord compression, followed by postoperative stereotactic body radiation therapy to T2 to T3 (35 Gy/5 fractions) in January 2021. In February 2021, she received palliative radiation therapy (20 Gy/5 fractions) to T9 to T12 for a T11 vertebral body metastasis with epidural extension. From January to August 2021, she was treated with gemcitabine, and in September 2021, she received her first dose of liposomal doxorubicin. Two weeks later, she developed progressive bilateral lower extremity numbness, pain, weakness, and imbalance, prompting emergent evaluation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings demonstrated extensive spinal cord edema extending from T2 to the conus and a posterior ring-enhancing intramedullary lesion at T9 to T10 without any mass effect (Figure 1). Because the intramedullary lesion appeared atypical for malignant disease given the lack of mass effect, she was prescribed high-dose steroids while further workup was pursued. Lumbar puncture showed no malignant cells. Positron emission tomographic-computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan demonstrated multifocal intensely F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid disease, but only mild uptake from T9 to T12 and no definitive FDG-avidity at the intramedullary lesion. Her symptoms remained stable with steroid treatment and a plan was made to repeat an MRI of the spine in 6 to 8 weeks.

options.B: Radiation recall myelopathy: continue steroids, discontinue doxorubicin
options.C: Radiation necrosis: continue steroids, add bevacizumab
options.D: Spinal cord infarct: underlying cause workup, supportive care

distractors: Radiation necrosis: continue steroids, add bevacizumab
Spinal cord infarct: underlying cause workup, supportive care
explanation: Given this patient’s metastatic disease, the initial concern was an intramedullary metastasis. However, the lack of mass effect on imaging and the atypical pattern of spread for uterine leiomyosarcoma suggested a possible alternative process. Spinal cord infarct was considered, although thought to be less likely given the acute enhancement, degree of edema, and lack of correlation with arterial territories. Although the ring enhancement with intense surrounding edema resembled radiation necrosis, the affected region only received a conventional palliative radiotherapy dose, too low to cause radiation necrosis. The timing of symptom onset in relation to her first doxorubicin infusion and the location of the lesion in the prior radiation field raised concern for radiation recall myelopathy. Given the stability of her symptoms upon treatment with steroids, negative results on lumbar puncture for malignant disease, lack of FDG-avidity of the T9 to T10 lesion on PET/CT, and timing of symptoms in the context of recent liposomal doxorubicin administration, the multidisciplinary consensus was in favor of radiation recall myelopathy. The risk of delaying irradiation if this were a metastasis vs the risk of irradiation causing further compromise if this were radiation recall myelopathy was discussed with the patient, and the decision was made to continue steroids with close clinical and radiographic surveillance. Radiation recall is a rare and poorly understood phenomenon that was initially described in 1959.1Generally occurring months to years after radiation therapy, radiation recall refers to an inflammatory reaction in a previously irradiated region following systemic therapy administration.2The incidence is challenging to estimate given that most data comes from case reports, with estimates ranging from 2% to 9%.1,3,4Although radiation recall reactions of the skin are the most common manifestation, additional studies have described inflammatory reactions in other tissues, including the lung (pneumonitis following gemcitabine), muscles (myositis after cyclophosphamide), and spine (myelitis following capecitabine, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, dabrafenib, or pembrolizumab).5-7Although doxorubicin has previously been implicated in radiation recall,4to our knowledge, this is the first report specifically describing doxorubicin-associated recall myelopathy. Of note, liposomal doxorubicin has superior central nervous system penetrance than standard doxorubicin, which may increase the risk of recall myelopathy. Prior reports of radiation recall–associated myelopathy have revealed certain associated radiographic findings. It is common to see a primary ring-enhancing lesion in the prior radiation field, as well as T1-weighted hyperintense marrow signal changes in adjacent vertebrae.8Spinal cord swelling and T2-signal abnormalities, predominantly involving the central cord, demonstrating longitudinal cord edema extending outside the radiation field has also been observed.8,9The etiology of this edema is unknown but could be owing to an extensive nonimmune inflammatory reaction.7 There is no standard treatment paradigm for radiation recall. At a minimum, the precipitating systemic agent should be held. Although there has also been success attributed to steroids, bevacizumab, immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, or hyperbaric oxygen,2,9,10it is unclear whether these agents are truly efficacious or whether clinical improvement or stabilization naturally ensues over time. Given its rarity, the prognosis remains unclear. Over the next month, the patient experienced mild clinical improvement in lower extremity weakness and pain but persistent urinary retention with high-dose steroid treatment. Findings on MRI 7 weeks after her initial scan demonstrated a decrease in the enhancing lesion and spinal cord edema (Figure 2). The lack of progression in the spine despite no oncologic therapy supported a diagnosis of radiation recall. She was discharged with instructions to taper steroid treatment with plans to initiate temozolomide.
